original_question: Find the smallest $p>0$ such that we can solve an $n x n$ linear system $Ax=b$ to high accuracy using $~ O(T_A*bar kappa_p)$ arithmetic operations, where $bar kappa_p$ is the $p$-averaged condition number of the singular values of $A$, whereas $T_A$ is either $n^2$ or $nnz(A)$.
target_in_paper: Section 2.4, "The effect of outlying singular values (or eigenvalues)", specifically Definition 2.5 together with Problem 2.6.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies that the paper asks for the smallest p>0, concerns solving an n×n linear system Ax=b to high accuracy, measures complexity in arithmetic operations of order \widetilde{O}(T_A\,\bar\kappa_p), uses the p-averaged condition number built from the singular values of A, and allows the two cost regimes T_A=n^2 or T_A=nnz(A).
missing_details: The paper states the bound with \widetilde{O}, not ordinary O; the polylogarithmic slack is part of the official formulation.
To make the question stand-alone, A should be specified as an invertible n×n matrix with singular values \sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n>0; otherwise \bar\kappa_p is not defined as in the paper.
The definition of the p-averaged condition number is missing: for finite p, \bar\kappa_p:=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\sigma_i/\sigma_n)^p\right)^{1/p}, and \bar\kappa_\infty:=\sigma_1/\sigma_n.

The quantifiers are implicit in the draft. The paper's problem is about an algorithmic guarantee for general linear systems, i.e. for arbitrary invertible A and right-hand side b, not for some special instance.
The phrase "to high accuracy" is left informal in the paper itself; a faithful rewrite should preserve that phrase rather than replacing it by a new error notion.
The problem is about arithmetic-operation complexity, not bit complexity; the nearby bit-complexity questions are separate Problems 2.9 and 2.10.
Although the subsection title mentions "singular values (or eigenvalues)", Problem 2.6 itself is stated only in terms of singular values of A.

The paper does not impose symmetry, positive semidefiniteness, or any other structural restriction on A in the problem statement; the PSD case appears only in the discussion of known partial progress.
If one wants the statement fully self-contained, nnz(A) should be identified as the number of nonzero entries of A, and T_A should be described as either the dense cost n^2 or the sparse cost nnz(A).
The paper notes the monotonicity \bar\kappa_{p_1}\leq \bar\kappa_{p_2} for p_1<p_2; this is the reason the question asks for the smallest p.
refined_question: What is the smallest real number p>0 such that, for every invertible n×n matrix A with singular values \sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n>0 and every right-hand side b, the linear system Ax=b can be solved to high accuracy using \widetilde{O}(T_A\,\bar\kappa_p) arithmetic operations, where \bar\kappa_p:=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\sigma_i/\sigma_n)^p\right)^{1/p} for p<\infty, \bar\kappa_\infty:=\sigma_1/\sigma_n, and T_A is either n^2 or nnz(A) (the number of nonzero entries of A)?
justification: The draft is an almost verbatim paraphrase of Problem 2.6 in Section 2.4, not of any broader neighboring problem. The essential nearby context is Definition 2.5, which introduces the p-averaged condition number from the ordered singular values and notes the monotonicity in p, directly motivating the search for the smallest admissible p. The discussion immediately after Problem 2.6 records the current partial progress: for T_A=n^2, the paper reports results for any p>1/2 in general and p>1/4 for psd systems, while for T_A=nnz(A) it says it is unclear whether any such result is possible for p<\infty. That confirms that your draft is targeting exactly Problem 2.6, and not the neighboring questions about outliers, random matrices, or bit complexity.
